must: Meet WCAG AA contrast ratios (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text/UI components) in every stated color mode.
avoid: Shipping a palette validated only in the designer's own light-mode preview, never checked against dark mode or actual small text sizes.

must: Give every interactive element a visible, distinct keyboard focus indicator.
avoid: Removing default focus outlines via CSS reset without supplying a replacement.

must: Provide text alternatives (alt text, aria-label) for meaningful non-text content.
avoid: Decorative images and meaningful icons treated identically, with either both or neither getting alt text.

must: Ensure logical, linear tab order matches the visual reading order.
avoid: Using positive tabindex values or CSS reordering that visually reorders content without reordering the DOM/tab sequence.

must: Support text resizing up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
avoid: Fixed-height containers that clip text when the user increases browser font size.

must: Design and verify layouts at a genuine mobile width (375px) as a first-class breakpoint, not an afterthought scaled down from desktop.
avoid: A desktop-only layout with everything simply shrunk, producing illegibly small text and cramped touch targets.

must: Let content reflow (wrap, stack) at narrow widths rather than triggering unintended horizontal scroll.
avoid: Fixed-width elements or `min-width` values wider than the viewport causing the whole page to scroll sideways.

must: Use relative units (rem, %, fr) for layout and type sizing rather than hard pixel values throughout.
avoid: Pixel-locked component widths that don't adapt across the full range of supported viewports.

must: Collapse multi-column data tables to a stacked or horizontally-scrollable pattern on narrow screens.
avoid: A 10-column table rendered unchanged at 375px width, forcing the whole page to scroll.

must: Test and specify tablet/mid-width (768-1024px) behavior explicitly, not just mobile and desktop extremes.
avoid: A layout that jumps awkwardly between a mobile stack and a desktop grid with no considered mid-point.

must: Show a loading/pending state for any operation likely to exceed ~300ms.
avoid: A UI that appears frozen with no feedback while a network call or heavy computation runs.

must: Use skeleton loaders or optimistic UI for predictable content shapes rather than a blank screen or spinner-only wait.
avoid: A full-screen spinner for a view whose eventual layout is already known, wasting the wait with no context.

must: Paginate, virtualize, or lazy-load long lists rather than rendering everything at once.
avoid: Rendering thousands of DOM nodes for a single unbounded list with no windowing.

must: Defer loading of below-the-fold images and non-critical assets.
avoid: Eagerly loading every image on a long page regardless of scroll position.

must: Debounce or throttle expensive handlers tied to high-frequency events (scroll, resize, keystroke-triggered search).
avoid: Firing a full re-render or network request on every single keystroke or scroll pixel.

must: Use one consistent spacing scale (e.g. 4/8px increments) across the entire product.
avoid: Arbitrary one-off margin/padding values that don't align to any shared scale, causing visual drift between screens.

must: Reuse the same component for the same semantic purpose everywhere (one button style per priority tier, one card pattern per content type).
avoid: Multiple visually-different buttons or cards serving the identical role in different parts of the product.

must: Apply the same interaction pattern for the same gesture everywhere (e.g. swipe always means the same thing across the app).
avoid: The same gesture triggering different, contradictory actions depending on which screen the user is on.

must: Keep terminology consistent for the same concept across every screen and every piece of copy.
avoid: Calling the same entity a 'Project' on one screen and a 'Workspace' on another.

must: Apply the chosen border-radius, shadow, and elevation tokens uniformly rather than per-component judgment calls.
avoid: Mixing sharp and heavily-rounded corners across sibling components with no systematic reason.

must: Make the current location in the navigation always visually clear (active state, breadcrumb, highlighted tab).
avoid: A nav bar with no indication of which section the user is currently in.

must: Keep primary navigation to a small, stable set of top-level destinations (roughly 5-7 max for tab/rail patterns).
avoid: A primary nav that grows unbounded as features are added, forcing overflow menus for core destinations.

must: Ensure every screen has a clear, obvious way back (browser back, explicit back button, or breadcrumb) — no dead ends.
avoid: Modal or drill-down flows that trap the user with no visible exit.

must: Make deep-linkable views actually reflect their state in the URL where the platform supports it (web).
avoid: A multi-step or filtered view whose URL never changes, making it impossible to share or reload a specific state.

must: Provide a visible search entry point once content volume passes roughly a screenful.
avoid: Forcing users to scroll through a long unstructured list with no way to search or filter.

must: Give every input a visible, persistently-associated label (not placeholder-only).
avoid: Placeholder text used as the only label, which disappears the moment the user starts typing.

must: Validate inline, as close to the offending field as possible, with a specific message.
avoid: A single generic 'form has errors' banner at the top with no indication of which fields or why.

must: Preserve user-entered data across a failed submit or navigation, never silently discard it.
avoid: A failed submission that clears the form, forcing the user to re-enter everything.

must: Mark required vs. optional fields explicitly and consistently (pick one convention, apply everywhere).
avoid: Inconsistent or absent required/optional marking that forces guesswork or a failed submit to discover.

must: Match input type/keyboard to the expected data (numeric keypad for phone numbers, email keyboard for email) on mobile.
avoid: A generic text keyboard for every field regardless of the data type expected.

must: State what went wrong in plain language and offer a concrete next step for every error.
avoid: Raw error codes, stack traces, or a bare 'Something went wrong' with no path forward.

must: Confirm the outcome of every user-initiated action (saved, sent, deleted) with a visible acknowledgment.
avoid: An action that silently succeeds or fails with zero visible confirmation either way.

must: Require explicit confirmation, naming what will be affected, before any destructive or irreversible action.
avoid: A single-click delete with no confirmation step, especially for bulk or irreversible operations.

must: Distinguish system errors (retry-able) from user errors (fixable input) in both tone and recovery action offered.
avoid: Treating a network timeout and a validation failure with the identical generic error message.

must: Offer offline/network-loss messaging distinct from a generic error when connectivity is the actual cause.
avoid: Showing a misleading 'server error' message when the real cause is the user's own lost connection.

must: Define an explicit, helpful empty state (icon/illustration, message, next action) for every list or collection view.
avoid: A blank screen with no explanation the first time a user has no data yet.

must: Write microcopy (button labels, tooltips, errors) in plain, specific, active language.
avoid: Vague labels like 'Submit' or 'OK' where a specific verb ('Save Draft', 'Delete 3 Items') would remove ambiguity.

must: Truncate long content predictably (with ellipsis + full text on hover/expand) rather than letting it break layout.
avoid: Unbounded text silently overflowing its container or forcing layout reflow across sibling elements.

must: Keep a comfortable reading measure (roughly 50-75 characters per line) for any substantial body text.
avoid: Full-viewport-width paragraphs on wide desktop screens forcing very long, fatiguing line lengths.

must: Use sentence case consistently for UI labels unless the product has an explicit, deliberate title-case brand voice.
avoid: Randomly mixed case conventions across buttons, headings, and menu items within the same product.

must: Size every interactive control at least 44x44px (iOS) / 48x48dp (Android), including invisible padding, not just the visible glyph.
avoid: Icon buttons sized to their 16-20px glyph alone with no padding expanding the hit area.

must: Leave adequate spacing between adjacent tappable targets (roughly 8px minimum) to prevent mis-taps.
avoid: Tightly packed icon buttons or list-row actions with no gap, especially on mobile.

must: Keep primary mobile actions within comfortable thumb reach (lower half of the screen) where the platform convention allows it.
avoid: Placing the single most-used action in a far top corner on a large-screen mobile device.

must: Provide larger touch targets for destructive or hard-to-undo actions rather than smaller, easy-to-mis-tap ones.
avoid: A tiny delete icon squeezed next to other icons where a slip becomes destructive.

must: Ensure hover-only affordances (desktop) have a touch-equivalent reveal method on mobile.
avoid: Actions that only appear on :hover with no tap/long-press equivalent, making them undiscoverable on touch devices.

must: Match information density to the tool's actual usage pattern — dense for daily power-user tools, spacious for infrequent/consumer use.
avoid: A dashboard-dense layout applied to a casual consumer app used a few minutes a week, overwhelming the user.

must: Let users scan a data table's key column(s) without horizontal scrolling on its primary target viewport.
avoid: The single most important column requiring a horizontal scroll to even see on first load.

must: Use consistent row heights and column alignment (numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned) in dense tabular views.
avoid: Inconsistent alignment that makes columns of numbers hard to scan and compare at a glance.

must: Offer a density toggle (comfortable/compact) when a tool genuinely serves both power users and occasional users.
avoid: Forcing every user into one fixed density regardless of how differently they actually use the tool.

must: Progressively disclose secondary detail (expand-on-demand) rather than showing every field for every row at once.
avoid: A table showing 20+ columns simultaneously when most rows only need 5-6 for a typical task.
